L4  /  Pathological basis of oral & systemic disease

Healing and Repair

Inflammation clears the damage; this lecture is about what fills the gap afterwards. Whether a tissue truly heals or is merely patched with scar depends on the cells it is made of — and the tooth socket is where you will watch the whole process play out.

Lecturer
Dr Joseph Ryan
Sections
22
Core reading
Underwood’s Ch. 5
Builds on
L2 cell injury → L3 inflammation
01

Cell types by regenerative capacity

Whether a tissue can heal at all is decided before the injury happens.

Lecture 2 introduced this classification; healing depends on it completely. A tissue made of labile cells can restore itself perfectly. A tissue made of permanent cells cannot, and must be patched with scar instead. Everything in this lecture follows from that.

Type 1

Labile cells

Divide throughout life. Continuously lost and continuously replaced — surface epithelia, gut lining, bone marrow.

Type 2

Stable cells

Divide when needed. Normally quiescent, but able to re-enter the cell cycle after injury — liver, kidney, fibroblasts.

Type 3

Permanent cells

Divide only during foetal life. Once destroyed they are gone for good — neurons, cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle.

A patient sustains an identical-depth burn to the epidermis and to cardiac muscle. Why do the outcomes differ so completely?

The epidermis is made of labile cells that divide throughout life, so it can fully regenerate with no residual defect. Cardiac muscle is made of permanent cells that divide only during foetal life; the lost myocytes cannot be replaced, so the defect is filled by fibrous scar — structurally present but functionally useless, and non-contractile.

From the lecture slides
02

Stem cells

The cells that make regeneration possible in the first place.

Stem cell

A cell that retains the ability to divide and, in the fullest case, to form a complete organism. Stem cells are the reservoir that labile and stable tissues draw on whenever cells are lost.

Two properties define them, and both matter clinically. They can self-renew, producing more stem cells so the reservoir is never exhausted, and they can differentiate into the mature cell types the tissue needs. How many types they can become is called potency, and it is the subject of the next section.

High yield

Totipotent cells can form all cells of the embryo and the placenta. This is the only grade that includes the supporting tissues — and it is the distinction most often tested against pluripotency.

03

The four grades of potency

Totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent, unipotent — a narrowing of options.

Potency falls as development proceeds. Each step down the ladder trades flexibility for specialisation, and the loss is one-way under normal conditions.

GradeCan formNote
TotipotentAll cells of the embryo and the placentaThe only grade that includes supporting tissue
PluripotentAll cells of the three embryonic layers, but not the supporting tissue of the embryoEctoderm, mesoderm, endoderm
MultipotentA number of cell typesTypically within one lineage, e.g. haematopoietic
UnipotentOnly one cell typeStill self-renewing — that is what keeps it a stem cell
What exactly can a totipotent cell do that a pluripotent cell cannot?

Form the supporting tissue of the embryo — the placenta. A pluripotent cell can make every cell of the three embryonic germ layers, so it can build the whole body, but it cannot produce the extra-embryonic supporting tissue.

From the lecture slides
04

Where the stem cells are

Tucked into protected niches, away from the surface being worn away.

Stem cells sit in niches — sheltered positions where they are least likely to be damaged by the wear the tissue is exposed to. Two examples from the lecture make the pattern obvious.

Epidermis

The basal layer

Immediately adjacent to the basement membrane — the deepest layer, furthest from the abrasive surface.

Intestinal mucosa

The bottom of the crypts

Near the base of the crypts, well below the villus tips where cells are constantly shed.

The pattern

In both tissues the stem cells sit at the furthest point from the surface. Daughter cells migrate outwards as they mature and are shed from the exposed edge. This is also why a deep burn or ulcer heals so much worse than a superficial one — it destroys the niche itself, and with it the tissue's capacity to regenerate.

Why does a superficial abrasion heal without a scar, while a deep burn scars?

A superficial abrasion leaves the basal layer — and therefore the stem cell niche — intact, so the epidermis regenerates completely. A deep burn destroys the basal layer across the wound, so there is no local reservoir to regenerate from; the defect is filled by granulation tissue and scar instead, with epithelium creeping in only from the surviving margins.

From the lecture slides
05

Stem cells in dentistry

Tissue engineering and periodontal regeneration.

The lecture points to stem cell research as the reason this topic appears in a dental pathology course. The periodontium is a good target: it is a composite of several tissues — cementum, periodontal ligament and alveolar bone — and once destroyed by periodontitis it does not regenerate on its own. Conventional treatment arrests the disease but produces repair, not regeneration: a long junctional epithelium rather than a new attachment apparatus.

Why this matters clinically

The aim of periodontal regenerative therapy is to shift the outcome from the repair column into the healing column — to rebuild a true attachment rather than patch the defect with scar. That is exactly the healing-versus-repair distinction of the next section, applied to a tissue you will treat.

Reading: Han et al. 2014, Stem cells, tissue engineering and periodontal regeneration, Australian Dental Journal 59(1 Suppl):117–130.

06

Healing versus repair

The single most important distinction in this lecture.

Healing

Regeneration

Complete restoration with no, or minimal, residual defect. There is loss of part of the labile cell population, but the tissue that returns is the tissue that was there before.

Repair

Organisation

Restoration with fibrovascular connective tissue. There is loss of specialised cell populations — the gap is filled, but with something less capable than the original.

Terminology warning — read this twice

The two standard textbooks use these words differently, and the lecture flags it explicitly:

  • In Robbins, “healing” is an umbrella term covering both regeneration and repair.
  • In Underwood’s, “healing” is used synonymously with regeneration — i.e. as the opposite of repair.

This lecture follows Underwood’s. If a question seems contradictory, check which convention it is using before answering.

A tissue is restored with fibrovascular connective tissue. Healing or repair — and what has been lost?

Repair. Fibrovascular connective tissue is the signature of organisation. What has been lost is the specialised cell population — the tissue is structurally continuous again but functionally poorer, because scar cannot do the job the original cells did.

From the lecture slides
07

Healing: the process

Following an abrasion injury from intact skin back to intact skin.

The lecture traces regeneration through a superficial abrasion, where the basal layer survives and the epidermis can rebuild itself completely.

  1. Normal skin
    Intact epidermis over an intact basement membrane.
  2. Abrasion injury
    The surface layers are scraped away, exposing the tissue beneath.
  3. A scab forms
    A layer of fibrin covers the defect. Its job is to protect the epidermis as it grows to cover the gap underneath.
  4. Cells proliferate and migrate
    Epidermal cells spread out as a thin sheet from the wound edges until the defect is covered.
  5. Proliferation stops
    They stop proliferating once they form a confluent layer — the mechanism is contact inhibition, covered next.
  6. The epidermis is rebuilt
    Once the sheet is in place, the epidermis is rebuilt from the base upwards until full thickness is restored.
High yield

The scab is not just debris — it is a fibrin layer that protects the regenerating epidermis underneath. Epithelium migrates beneath the scab, not over it. This is the same principle that makes the blood clot so important in tooth socket healing later in this lecture.

From the lecture slides
08

Contact inhibition

The stop signal — and what happens when it is lost.

Contact inhibition

Cells stop proliferating when they come into contact with one another. It is the mechanism that halts regeneration at exactly the right moment: once the sheet is confluent, the wound is covered, and further division would serve no purpose.

When the brake fails

In neoplasia these control mechanisms are lost, which allows the continued proliferation of tumour cells. The same machinery that makes ordered healing possible, when it fails, is what permits a tumour to keep growing past the point where normal tissue would have stopped.

What stops epidermal cells proliferating once they have covered a wound, and what is the consequence of losing that control?

Contact inhibition — cells stop dividing once they contact one another and form a confluent layer. In neoplasia this control is lost, permitting the continued, unregulated proliferation of tumour cells.

09

Organisation: the process

When the tissue cannot regenerate, it is replaced.

Organisation

Repair of specialised tissues by the formation of mature fibrovascular connective tissue. This is the process that produces a scar.

  1. Fibrin deposition
    The defect fills with fibrin, providing a provisional scaffold.
  2. Granulation tissue formation
    New capillaries and fibroblasts grow into the fibrin.
  3. Removal of dead tissue
    By neutrophils and macrophages — the debris must be cleared before the defect can be rebuilt.
  4. The granulation tissue contracts
    Reducing the volume of the defect that has to be filled.
  5. Collagen accumulates to form the scar
    The final product: mature fibrous tissue in place of the specialised tissue that was lost.
Link back to L3A

Granulation tissue is the same tissue you met in acute inflammation — new capillaries, fibroblasts and inflammatory cells in a loose matrix. Note the persistent confusion trap: granulation tissue has nothing to do with granulomas from Lecture 3B, and nothing to do with granular appearance of pus.

From the lecture slides
10

Wound contraction and scarring

Myofibroblasts pull the wound closed — usefully, then harmfully.

Contraction aims to reduce the volume of tissue that has to be repaired. A smaller defect needs less collagen and closes faster, so contraction is initially helpful.

Mechanism

Contraction results from the contraction of myofibroblasts in the granulation tissue. These are attached to each other and to the adjacent matrix components, so when they shorten, the whole wound bed is drawn inwards.

Collagen is secreted and forms a scar, replacing the lost specialised tissues. Infection and associated inflammation are liable to increase scarring — a clinically useful point, since it means wound infection has a lasting cosmetic and functional cost, not just a short-term one.

When contraction goes too far

Stenosis

Narrowing of a lumen

Narrowing or obstruction due to a stricture of a tube lumen — oesophagus, bile duct, bowel.

Contracture

Permanent shortening

Tissue distortion resulting in permanent shortening of a muscle, limiting the range of movement.

After burns

Cosmetic & functional loss

Cosmetic damage and often impaired mobility due to contraction after burns to the skin.

Which cell drives wound contraction, and name two harmful consequences when it acts excessively.

The myofibroblast, contracting within the granulation tissue while attached to its neighbours and to the surrounding matrix. Excessive contraction causes stenosis (narrowing or obstruction of a tube lumen from a stricture) and contracture (tissue distortion with permanent shortening of a muscle); after skin burns it also causes cosmetic damage and impaired mobility.

11

Skin: healing by first intention

A clean, closely apposed wound — the surgeon's ideal.

First intention

The pattern seen in surgical incisions. There is very little damage to the tissues on either side of the cut, and close approximation of the wound edges enables prompt and uneventful healing.

  1. Incision
    A clean cut with minimal collateral tissue damage.
  2. Scab / eschar
    The narrow gap fills with fibrin and a scab forms over the surface.
  3. Capillaries proliferate
    Neovascularisation across the incision line.
  4. Fibroblasts migrate and secrete
    They migrate into the fibrin network and secrete collagen.
  5. Epithelium bridges the gap
    The surface is restored over a narrow, well-supported defect.
What never comes back

The elastic fibre network will not be reconstructed. Even in the best possible wound, under ideal conditions, the repaired tissue is not identical to the original — it lacks the elasticity of intact dermis. This is why even a fine surgical scar remains detectably different from the skin around it.

From the lecture slides
12

Skin: healing by second intention

Tissue has been lost, so the gap must be filled before it can be covered.

Where first intention deals with a clean line, second intention deals with a defect. The three opening features follow from that single difference.

Feature 1

Tissue loss

Substance is missing, not merely divided — there is a volume to be filled.

Feature 2

Gaping wound margins

The edges cannot be brought together, so the defect stays open.

Feature 3

Haemorrhage and infection

A large open surface bleeds more and is far more readily colonised.

How it proceeds

  1. Phagocytosis of debris
    Necrotic tissue and contaminating material are cleared first.
  2. Granulation tissue
    Fills the defect from the base upwards — this is the step that first intention barely needs.
  3. Epithelial regeneration
    Epithelium migrates across only once there is a granulation bed to migrate over.
 First intentionSecond intention
Typical causeSurgical incisionTissue loss — ulcer, avulsion, extraction socket
Wound edgesClosely apposedGaping
Tissue lostMinimalSubstantial
Granulation tissueScantAbundant — must fill the defect
ContractionLittleMarked
Infection riskLowHigh
ScarSmall, linearLarge, and liable to contract
High yield

The difference is not the mechanism — both use the same steps. It is the amount of tissue lost, and therefore how much granulation tissue is needed to fill the gap. Everything else, including the bigger scar and the greater contraction, follows from that.

Why does a wound healing by second intention contract so much more than a surgical incision?

Because there is real tissue loss and the margins gape, so a large volume of granulation tissue must fill the defect. Contraction is driven by myofibroblasts within that granulation tissue, so the more granulation tissue is present, the greater the contraction — hence the larger scar and the risk of contracture. A surgical incision has closely apposed edges and almost no defect to fill.

From the lecture slides
13

Mechanism: cytokines and growth factors

A complex interplay, with two rules that make it manageable.

The lecture is explicit that this is a complex interplay of cytokines, and gives two warnings that stop you trying to memorise a clean one-to-one map:

Rule 1

One cell, many cytokines

The same cell may produce many cytokines.

Rule 2

One cytokine, many jobs

Most cytokines have many functions.

Initiating signals

Hypoxia Growth factors from platelet degranulation

The keratinocyte axis

Platelets, macrophages and fibroblasts produce cytokines including epidermal growth factor (EGF) and keratinocyte growth factor (KGF). These growth factors stimulate keratinocyte proliferation and mobility — that is, they drive exactly the migration and division described in the healing process earlier.

Connecting it up

Hypoxia is an initiating signal, and hypoxia is also what tissue at the centre of a defect experiences once its blood supply is cut. The wound therefore signals its own need for new vessels, which is the subject of the next section.

14

Angiogenesis

New vessels — without them nothing else can proceed.

VEGF

Vascular endothelial growth factor

Produced by keratinocytes and macrophages.

PDGF

Platelet-derived growth factor

Produced by platelets, macrophages and keratinocytes.

Together these lead to activation of macrophages, proliferation of fibroblasts and matrix production — the three things that turn an empty defect into granulation tissue.

From the lecture slides
15

Myofibroblasts, TGF-β and abnormal scars

One growth factor, and the two ways scarring goes wrong.

Transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) controls myofibroblasts and collagen formation — that is, it governs both the contraction of the wound and the material that fills it. Abnormalities in this control can result in hypertrophic scars or keloid.

 Hypertrophic scarKeloid
ExtentStays within the original wound boundaryGrows beyond the original wound boundary
CourseOften regresses over timePersists; commonly recurs after excision
Underlying problemExcess collagen deposition, under abnormal TGF-β control
A way to keep them apart

Hypertrophic means overgrown — but still inside its own borders. Keloid spills over the edge. If the scar has crossed the line of the original wound, it is a keloid.

16

Healing of mucosal ulcers

The oral relevance — and what happens when it never finishes.

  1. Bleeding, then covering by fibrin
    The same protective fibrin layer as the cutaneous scab.
  2. Removal of necrotic tissue by macrophages
    Debridement before rebuilding.
  3. Granulation tissue formation
    Fills the base of the ulcer.
  4. Epithelial regeneration from the ulcer edges
    Epithelium can only advance from surviving margins — which is why a wide ulcer takes disproportionately longer to close than a narrow one.
Chronic ulceration

When the cause is not removed, the ulcer enters a cycle of alternating ulceration and repair, with ongoing destruction of tissue. Fibrous scar tissue replaces muscle, and the scar will contract. In a hollow organ such as the stomach, that contraction is what produces stenosis — the link back to wound contraction earlier in this lecture.

Straight from Lecture 3B

This is the histological counterpart of ulcerative inflammation. The reason chronic ulcers scar so heavily is the same reason chronic inflammation does: damage and healing are running at the same time, indefinitely.

Why does a chronic ulcer produce so much more scarring than an acute one that heals in a week?

Because the injurious agent is never removed, so the ulcer alternates between ulceration and repair indefinitely. Each cycle deposits more collagen while tissue continues to be destroyed, so fibrous scar progressively replaces specialised tissue such as muscle, and the accumulated scar then contracts — producing stenosis in a tubular organ.

From the lecture slides
17

Healing of bone

The one specialised tissue that regenerates rather than scars.

Bone is exceptional. Most specialised tissues are repaired with fibrous scar; bone rebuilds itself as bone, passing through a temporary, mechanically inferior form on the way.

  1. Haematoma
    Blood from ruptured vessels in the periosteum and bone marrow cavity fills the fracture site. The haematoma is organised and dead bone is removed.
  2. Callus — woven bone
    Internal and external callus (a mass of new bone) is formed. This is woven bone, laid down in an irregular pattern — quick to make, but weak.
  3. Lamellar bone and remodelling
    The woven bone is replaced by lamellar bone, then remodelled according to the direction of mechanical stress.
Why is woven bone laid down first if lamellar bone is stronger?

Because it can be produced quickly. Woven bone has an irregular pattern and is mechanically weak, but it bridges the fracture and provides provisional stability far sooner than organised bone could be built. It is then replaced by lamellar bone and remodelled according to the direction of mechanical stress — speed first, strength second.

From the lecture slides
18

When bone healing goes wrong

Five factors, and three named clinical situations.

Factors affecting bone healing

FactorConsequence
MobilityFibrous union — a false joint forms instead of bony continuity
Interposed soft tissuesMay lead to non-union — tissue physically blocks the bone ends from meeting
MisalignmentImpairs function, with risk of osteoarthrosis in adjacent joints
InfectionPrevents or delays union
Pre-existing bone diseaseCompromises the tissue’s ability to respond at all
High yield

Mobility → fibrous union → false joint. This is the mechanical reason fractures are immobilised. Movement at the fracture site prevents the callus from mineralising into a bony bridge, so fibrous tissue forms instead and the bone ends continue to move against one another.

Three named situations

Pathological

Pathological fracture

Fracture due to diseases of bone — either a primary bone disorder, or secondary involvement such as metastatic deposit. The bone fails under a load it should have tolerated.

Compound

Compound fracture

A fracture involving the overlying skin. The breach means the fracture site is exposed to the external environment — hence the markedly higher infection risk.

Therapeutic

Distraction osteogenesis

Healing exploited deliberately: the bone is cut and the segments slowly separated, so new bone forms continuously in the gap. Used in maxillofacial surgery to lengthen the jaw.

Dental relevance

A pathological fracture of the mandible is a recognised complication of MRONJ, osteomyelitis, radiotherapy and large cysts or tumours — all of which weaken bone to the point where normal function is enough to break it.

19

Liver, nerve and muscle

Three tissues, three very different answers.

Liver — three sources of regeneration

  1. Hepatocytes
    The mature cells themselves re-enter the cell cycle — classic stable cell behaviour.
  2. Liver progenitor (stem) cells
    A resident reserve population.
  3. Bone marrow-derived stem cells
    Recruited from outside the organ entirely.

Nervous tissue — the poorest performer

Central nervous system

The central nervous system does not repair effectively. Adult nerve cells may have a low replicative capacity, and the response to injury is gliosis — proliferation of glial cells, which fills the defect without restoring function. Gliosis is, in effect, the CNS equivalent of scarring.

Peripheral nerve has a connective tissue architecture that matters for repair, because an intact sheath gives a regenerating axon something to grow along:

Outer

Epineurium

The outer connective tissue layer of the nerve trunk.

Middle

Perineurium

Surrounds the fascicles that contain the nerve fibres.

Inner

Endoneurium

Loose connective tissue surrounding the individual nerve fibres.

Muscle — largely permanent

Muscle typeCapacity
CardiacPermanent cells — damaged muscle is replaced by scar tissue
SmoothPermanent cells, but vascular smooth muscle may differ, in that new vessels can be formed
Voluntary (skeletal)Limited capacity for regeneration from satellite cells
A partial escape

If only the contractile proteins are lost and the cell survives, it is possible to synthesise new ones within the old endomysium. The cell is not replaced — it is refitted inside its existing sheath. That is why damage confined to contractile protein recovers far better than damage that kills the fibre outright.

Why does a myocardial infarct leave a permanent functional deficit, while a comparable liver insult may not?

Cardiac muscle is made of permanent cells, so lost myocytes cannot be replaced and the area is filled with non-contractile scar tissue. The liver is a stable tissue with three sources of new cells — hepatocytes themselves, resident liver progenitor cells, and bone marrow-derived stem cells — so it can regenerate functioning parenchyma.

From the lecture slides
20

Healing of the tooth socket

The one you will watch happen, week by week.

Immediately: formation of a blood clot

Normal clotting mechanisms produce a loose clot that fills the bony and soft tissue socket. Platelets then retract the clot, expressing fluid so that it becomes harder and shrinks below the level of the adjacent soft tissues, pulling any mobile soft tissue inwards to reduce the area of clot exposed.

Two numbers worth memorising

Clot retraction is usually complete in 4 hours, and the clot surface changes from shiny to matt. After retraction the clot continues to stabilise by fibrin cross-linking — which is why avoiding rinsing is usually recommended for 24 hours. The post-operative instruction you will give every patient comes directly from this mechanism.

Stage by stage

TimeWhat is happening
4 hoursClot retraction usually complete; surface changes from shiny to matt; fibrin cross-linking continues
2 daysFibrinolysis has started; inflammatory cells emigrate into the clot
4 daysMacrophages remove debris; organisation of the clot begins; bacterial enzymes lyse surface fibrin; epithelial cells begin to grow below surface debris, over the intact clot
8 daysSocket filled with granulation tissue; superficial layers contain inflammatory cells; lamina dura still intact but resorption has begun
18 daysCollagen deposition; woven bone formation; osteogenic front advancing
6 weeksBone remodelling to lamellar bone; lamina dura still visible
Dry socket — the timing question

The risk of dry socket is highest at around 2 days: the stage when fibrinolysis has started but the clot is not yet well anchored to the wall. That combination — the clot being broken down while still poorly attached — is what allows it to be lost, exposing bare bone.

Why do you tell a patient not to rinse for 24 hours after an extraction?

Because clot retraction is only complete at about 4 hours, and after retraction the clot is still stabilising by fibrin cross-linking. Rinsing during this window can dislodge a clot that is not yet mechanically secure. Losing it exposes bone and produces a dry socket — the risk of which peaks at around 2 days, once fibrinolysis has begun but before the clot is firmly anchored to the socket wall.

From the lecture slides
21

Factors that affect healing and repair

Why two patients with identical wounds do not heal identically.

FactorWhy it impairs healing
AgeReduced capacity and cellular reserves
Disorders of nutritionImpaired protein synthesis — collagen cannot be made without substrate
Neoplastic disordersCompete for resources and impair the general response
Cushing’s syndrome & steroid therapyImmunosuppressive actions mean the consequences of injury or infection may be more severe; steroids also impair healing by interfering with the formation of granulation tissue, and thus with wound contraction
Diabetes mellitus & immunosuppressionInfection, immune suppression, impaired neutrophil function, ischaemia, neuropathy — several mechanisms at once
Vascular disturbanceWithout perfusion there is no oxygen, no cells and no substrate delivery
DenervationUnresponsiveness to repeated minor trauma, and lack of pain from infection or inflammation — so injury goes unnoticed and unprotected
High yield — steroids

Steroids get their own line in the lecture because they act twice: immunosuppression makes infection more severe, and they directly interfere with granulation tissue formation and therefore wound contraction. Both halves are examinable.

Why diabetes is the classic example

Diabetes hits nearly every requirement for healing simultaneously — perfusion (ischaemia), defence (impaired neutrophil function and immune suppression), and protection (neuropathy removes the pain that would normally prompt the patient to offload the wound). That convergence is what makes diabetic wound healing the standard case study, and why the lecture assigns Guo & DiPietro on the topic.

The lecture also raises psychological stress as a factor affecting wound healing, drawing on the same review.

Give two distinct mechanisms by which corticosteroid therapy impairs wound healing.

First, immunosuppression — the consequences of injury or infection become more severe. Second, a direct effect on repair: steroids interfere with the formation of granulation tissue, and therefore also impair wound contraction, since contraction depends on myofibroblasts within that granulation tissue.

From the lecture slides
22

Summary and glossary

The whole lecture on one screen.

The through-line

  1. Cell type sets the ceiling
    Labile and stable tissues can regenerate; permanent tissues cannot.
  2. Stem cells supply the raw material
    Graded by potency, and hidden in protected niches.
  3. Healing restores; repair replaces
    Healing leaves no significant defect. Repair leaves fibrovascular scar and loses specialised cells.
  4. Tissue loss decides first vs second intention
    Same mechanism, different amount of granulation tissue — and therefore different contraction and scarring.
  5. Growth factors run the process
    EGF and KGF for keratinocytes, VEGF and PDGF for vessels and matrix, TGF-β for myofibroblasts and collagen.
  6. Bone is the exception
    It regenerates as bone: haematoma, woven callus, lamellar bone, remodelled to load.
  7. The socket combines both
    Bone healing underneath, epithelial regeneration on top, with a clot that must be protected.
  8. Host factors modify everything
    Age, nutrition, steroids, diabetes, perfusion, innervation.

Glossary

Healing
Complete restoration with no, or minimal, residual defect; used synonymously with regeneration in Underwood’s.
Repair
Restoration with fibrovascular connective tissue, with loss of specialised cell populations.
Organisation
Repair of specialised tissues by the formation of mature fibrovascular connective tissue.
Granulation tissue
New capillaries, fibroblasts and inflammatory cells in a loose matrix — the tissue that fills a defect. Not a granuloma.
Contact inhibition
Cells stop proliferating on contact with one another; lost in neoplasia.
Myofibroblast
Contractile cell of granulation tissue, attached to its neighbours and to the matrix; drives wound contraction.
Stenosis
Narrowing or obstruction due to a stricture of a tube lumen.
Contracture
Tissue distortion resulting in permanent shortening of a muscle.
Keloid
Excessive scar extending beyond the boundary of the original wound.
Hypertrophic scar
Excessive scar remaining within the boundary of the original wound.
First intention
Healing of a wound with closely apposed edges and minimal tissue loss, e.g. a surgical incision.
Second intention
Healing of a wound with tissue loss and gaping margins, requiring granulation tissue to fill the defect.
Woven bone
Provisional bone with an irregular pattern, formed rapidly in callus.
Lamellar bone
Definitive layered bone, remodelled according to the direction of mechanical stress.
Callus
Mass of new bone, internal and external, formed at a fracture site.
Non-union
Failure of a fracture to unite, e.g. from interposed soft tissue.
Fibrous union
Union by fibrous tissue rather than bone, producing a false joint; caused by mobility.
Pathological fracture
Fracture due to disease of bone, either a primary bone disorder or secondary involvement.
Compound fracture
Fracture involving the overlying skin.
Gliosis
Proliferation of glial cells in response to CNS injury.
Epineurium
Outer connective tissue of a peripheral nerve.
Perineurium
Connective tissue surrounding fascicles containing nerve fibres.
Endoneurium
Loose connective tissue surrounding individual nerve fibres.
Satellite cells
Cells giving voluntary muscle its limited capacity for regeneration.
Dry socket
Loss or lysis of the extraction clot exposing bone; risk highest once fibrinolysis has begun but before the clot is well anchored.
Distraction osteogenesis
Surgical lengthening of bone by gradual separation of segments, with new bone forming in the gap.
Required reading

Underwood’s Pathology: a Clinical Approach (8th ed.), Simon Cross (2024), Chapter 5. Plus: Guo & DiPietro, Factors affecting wound healing, J Dent Res 89(3):219–229, 2010; Hupp, Ellis & Tucker (2014) Contemporary Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery 6th ed., pp. 251–259 (injury and healing of peripheral nerves); Cawson & Odell (2008) Cawson’s Essentials of Oral Pathology and Oral Medicine 7th ed., Appendix 6.1 p. 113; and Araujo et al. 2015, Alveolar socket healing: what can we learn?, Periodontology 2000, 68(1):122–124.
